questions.q: Why does a serum phosphate level poorly reflect the body's total phosphate stores?
ch: Most phosphate is stored in skeletal muscle as 2,3-DPG and is not exchangeable
Serum phosphate is held so tightly constant by PTH that it essentially never varies
Phosphate circulates almost entirely bound to albumin, so only a free fraction is measured
About 85% is stored in bone and only about 1% is extracellular
Roughly half of body phosphate is extracellular and half intracellular, so the pools cancel out
questions.exp: Phosphate is the body's main intracellular anion, and about 85% is stored in bone mineral with only about 1% extracellular — so the measured serum level can be normal while total-body stores are depleted.
why: 2,3-DPG is one of the compounds phosphate supports, not a storage depot; about 85% of stores sit in bone mineral.
PTH and FGF-23 are phosphaturic regulators, but serum phosphate varies widely — including large shifts with insulin, glucose, and refeeding.
Phosphate is the main intracellular anion; the module attributes the poor correlation to bone storage, not to albumin binding.
Only about 1% of phosphate is extracellular, so the two pools are nowhere near equal.

questions.q: Which serum phosphate value defines hypophosphatemia?
ch: A serum phosphate below 4.5 mg/dL
A serum phosphate above 4.5 mg/dL
A serum phosphate below 2.5 mg/dL
A serum phosphate below 8.0 mg/dL
A serum phosphate below 1.0 mg/dL
questions.exp: Hypophosphatemia is defined as a serum phosphate below 2.5 mg/dL; symptoms of hypophosphatemia typically appear once the phosphate falls below 1.0 mg/dL.
why: 4.5 mg/dL is the upper limit of normal; values above it define hyperphosphatemia.
A phosphate above 4.5 mg/dL is hyperphosphatemia, the opposite disorder.
8.0 mg/dL is far above the normal range, so this cutoff would include entirely normal phosphate levels.
Below 1.0 mg/dL is the threshold at which symptoms such as muscle weakness and respiratory failure appear, not the definition of the disorder.

questions.q: Hypophosphatemia arises through which three mechanisms?
ch: Transcellular shift, decreased gut absorption, and renal wasting
Increased bone resorption, hemolysis, and impaired renal excretion
Tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, and chronic kidney disease
Excess calcitriol, excess dietary intake, and volume contraction
Hypoparathyroidism, alkali ingestion, and hemodialysis
questions.exp: The module frames hypophosphatemia by three mechanisms: transcellular shift (refeeding, respiratory alkalosis, insulin/glucose), decreased gut absorption (malnutrition, antacids, vitamin D deficiency), and renal wasting (hyperparathyroidism, Fanconi, diuretics).
why: Massive cellular release such as hemolysis and impaired renal excretion cause hyperphosphatemia, not hypophosphatemia.
Tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, and CKD are the classic causes of hyperphosphatemia listed in this module.
Calcitriol is the absorptive hormone and would raise, not lower, the serum phosphate.
PTH is phosphaturic, so a low PTH raises serum phosphate; none of these are the module’s three mechanisms.

questions.q: Symptoms of hypophosphatemia characteristically appear once the level falls below 1.0 mg/dL. Which cluster of findings is expected?
ch: Diarrhea, hypercalcemia, and a suppressed PTH from oral supplementation
Tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, paresthesias, and pruritus from metastatic calcification
Kussmaul respirations, deep sighing hyperventilation, and a widened anion gap on chemistry
Vascular calcification, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and renal osteodystrophy
Muscle weakness, respiratory failure from diaphragm weakness, hemolysis, confusion, and impaired myocardial contractility
questions.exp: Once phosphate falls below 1.0 mg/dL, ATP and 2,3-DPG production suffer: muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure from diaphragm weakness, hemolysis, confusion, and impaired myocardial contractility.
why: Diarrhea is a common side effect of oral phosphate repletion rather than a manifestation of a low phosphate.
Those findings belong to hyperphosphatemia and largely reflect the hypocalcemia it causes.
Kussmaul breathing and a widened anion gap are the signature of severe metabolic acidosis, not of phosphate depletion.
Those are consequences of retained phosphate in CKD-MBD, the hyperphosphatemic side of this module.

questions.q: A malnourished man with heavy alcohol use is admitted after a week of almost no oral intake, and nutrition is about to be started. Which plan best reflects the module’s guidance?
ch: Advance calories slowly, replete phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and give thiamine with the carbohydrate load
Withhold all nutrition until the serum phosphate is above 4.5 mg/dL
Infuse calcium-containing fluids alongside the feeds to prevent metastatic calcification
Start full-calorie enteral feeding immediately and correct electrolytes only if symptoms develop
Give a phosphate binder with each meal to prevent a rise in the serum phosphate
questions.exp: Refeeding syndrome is the classic cause of dangerous hypophosphatemia: advance calories slowly, replete phosphate first along with potassium and magnesium, and give thiamine before or with the carbohydrate load.
why: 4.5 mg/dL is the upper limit of normal, and the module advances calories cautiously rather than withholding them until phosphate is supranormal.
Calcium-containing fluids are specifically avoided during phosphate repletion because of the precipitation risk.
Feeds are started low and slow precisely because a full carbohydrate load drives the life-threatening shifts of refeeding syndrome.
Binders are for CKD hyperphosphatemia; this patient is at risk of a dangerously low phosphate, not a high one.

questions.q: What is the key teaching point for a CKD patient starting calcium acetate as a phosphate binder?
ch: Take it between meals on an empty stomach for the best absorption
Take it at bedtime with a full glass of water each night
Take it only on dialysis days, one hour before the treatment
Take it with a high-dairy snack to improve palatability and tolerance
Take it with meals so that it binds dietary phosphate in the gut
questions.exp: Phosphate binders are taken WITH meals so they bind dietary phosphate in the gut — the module calls this a favorite NCLEX and boards discriminator. Calcium acetate also delivers a calcium load, so total elemental calcium is limited.
why: Binders act in the gut on food phosphate, so a dose taken between meals is wasted — a favorite boards discriminator.
Dosing at bedtime separates the binder from the meal whose phosphate it is supposed to bind.
Binders are dosed with meals every day; they are not tied to the dialysis schedule.
Dairy is one of the high-phosphate foods the module tells CKD patients to limit, along with cola, processed meats, and nuts.

questions.q: Hyperphosphatemia produces tetany, paresthesias, and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs. What explains these findings?
ch: They come from FGF-23 excess driving renal phosphate wasting
They are the manifestations of the hypocalcemia that the high phosphate causes
They result from phosphate itself acting as a direct neuromuscular stimulant
They reflect the depletion of ATP and 2,3-DPG inside muscle cells
They are caused by the accompanying hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
questions.exp: The symptoms of hyperphosphatemia are really the symptoms of the hypocalcemia it causes — tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, paresthesias, and metastatic calcification with pruritus.
why: FGF-23-mediated wasting produces chronically low phosphate, as in tumor-induced osteomalacia.
The module attributes these symptoms to the resultant hypocalcemia rather than to any direct excitatory effect of phosphate.
Impaired ATP and 2,3-DPG production is the mechanism behind hypophosphatemic weakness and hemolysis, not hyperphosphatemia.
Potassium and magnesium are tracked alongside phosphate, but the module ties these particular signs to a low calcium.

questions.q: A patient has a serum phosphate of 1.4 mg/dL. Which test best separates renal phosphate wasting from a transcellular shift?
ch: A serum PTH level interpreted on its own without urine studies
Urine phosphate or the fractional excretion of phosphate
A 25-OH vitamin D level to assess absorptive capacity
A serum calcium and magnesium panel drawn during repletion
An FGF-23 level as the initial screening test
questions.exp: A high urine phosphate, or a high fractional excretion of phosphate, alongside a low serum phosphate indicates renal loss rather than a shift — the module’s way of separating the shift, gut, and kidney mechanisms.
why: PTH helps define the mechanism alongside calcium, but it is the urine phosphate that proves the loss is renal.
Vitamin D is checked when decreased gut absorption is suspected, not to demonstrate renal wasting.
Calcium and magnesium must be tracked with phosphate during repletion, but they do not localize the loss to the kidney.
FGF-23 is reserved for unexplained chronic renal phosphate wasting once urine studies already point to the kidney.

questions.q: Which laboratory tetrad should you expect in tumor lysis syndrome?
ch: Low phosphate, high potassium, high uric acid, and low calcium
High phosphate, high potassium, low uric acid, and high calcium
High phosphate, high potassium, high uric acid, and low calcium
Low phosphate, low potassium, low uric acid, and high calcium
High phosphate, low potassium, high calcium, and low uric acid
questions.exp: The tumor lysis tetrad is up phosphate, up potassium, up uric acid, down calcium — prevented with hydration plus rasburicase or allopurinol, and treated with dialysis when severe.
why: Phosphate rises in tumor lysis from massive cellular release; it does not fall.
Uric acid rises and calcium falls, which is why prophylaxis targets the urate load with rasburicase or allopurinol.
That is the mirror image of the tetrad; tumor lysis releases intracellular contents and raises phosphate, potassium, and uric acid.
Potassium rises and calcium falls in tumor lysis, so this combination inverts both of them.

questions.q: A patient has a low serum phosphate, an elevated serum calcium, and an elevated PTH. What does this pattern indicate?
ch: Vitamin D deficiency with decreased gut phosphate absorption
CKD-mineral and bone disorder from retained phosphate
Refeeding syndrome after a prolonged period of being NPO
Primary hyperparathyroidism causing phosphaturic renal phosphate loss
Tumor lysis syndrome with massive intracellular release
questions.exp: Phosphate and calcium are inversely related through PTH and FGF-23: a low phosphate with a high calcium and a high PTH points to primary hyperparathyroidism, in which phosphaturic PTH wastes phosphate in the urine.
why: Vitamin D deficiency reduces both calcium and phosphate absorption, so the calcium would not be elevated.
CKD-MBD features retained, high phosphate stimulating FGF-23 and PTH — not hypophosphatemia with hypercalcemia.
Refeeding shifts phosphate into cells but does not raise calcium or PTH; its tip-off is the recent carbohydrate load.
Tumor lysis raises phosphate and lowers calcium, the opposite of this pattern.

questions.q: Which set of findings defines metabolic acidosis?
ch: A PaCO2 above 45 mmHg with an arterial pH below 7.35
A PaCO2 below 35 mmHg with an arterial pH above 7.45
A primary fall in HCO3- below about 22 mEq/L with an arterial pH below 7.35
A normal arterial pH with a widened anion gap and a normal bicarbonate
A primary rise in HCO3- above 26 mEq/L with an arterial pH above 7.45
questions.exp: Metabolic acidosis is a primary metabolic process lowering HCO3- (typically below 22 mEq/L) and arterial pH (below 7.35), driven by acid gain, bicarbonate loss, or impaired renal acid excretion.
why: A primary rise in PaCO2 from inadequate alveolar ventilation defines respiratory acidosis.
A primary fall in PaCO2 from alveolar hyperventilation defines respiratory alkalosis.
The disorder is defined by a low bicarbonate and a low pH; a normal pH with a normal bicarbonate is not the primary process.
A primary elevation in bicarbonate with alkalemia is metabolic alkalosis.

questions.q: How is the serum anion gap calculated, and what is its normal range?
ch: Measured osmolality minus calculated osmolality, normally 8-12 mEq/L
Na - (Cl + HCO3), normally 8-12 mEq/L
Na + K - Cl, normally 8-12 mEq/L
(Na + K) - (Cl + HCO3), normally 20-24 mEq/L
1.5 x HCO3 + 8, normally 8-12 mEq/L
questions.exp: The anion gap is Na - (Cl + HCO3) with a normal range of 8-12 mEq/L; it forks the differential into a high anion gap acidosis from unmeasured acids versus a normal-gap hyperchloremic acidosis from bicarbonate loss.
why: That is the osmolar gap, ordered when toxic alcohols are suspected.
Na + K - Cl is the urine anion gap used to work up a non-gap acidosis, not the serum anion gap.
The module’s gap omits potassium and its normal range is 8-12 mEq/L.
1.5 x HCO3 + 8 is Winter’s formula for the expected PaCO2, not the anion gap.

questions.q: MUDPILES lists the causes of which category of metabolic acidosis?
ch: Metabolic alkalosis maintained by chloride and potassium depletion
High anion gap metabolic acidosis from unmeasured acids
Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal bicarbonate retention
Mixed acid-base disorders detected by the delta-delta ratio
Normal anion gap hyperchloremic acidosis from bicarbonate loss
questions.exp: MUDPILES — Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol/Paraldehyde, Iron/Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates — is the high anion gap differential driven by unmeasured acids.
why: MUDPILES has nothing to do with alkalosis; it lists unmeasured-acid causes of acidosis.
MUDPILES is a metabolic mnemonic, not a description of a respiratory disorder.
The delta-delta ratio uncovers a second process inside a gap acidosis; MUDPILES names the gap causes themselves.
The non-gap causes follow USED CARP — practically, diarrhea, RTA, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.

questions.q: A patient has a serum HCO3 of 12 mEq/L. Which formula gives the expected PaCO2, and what does deviation from it mean?
ch: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 plus or minus 2; a value outside that range means a coexisting respiratory disorder
Expected PaCO2 = Na - (Cl + HCO3); a value outside that range means unmeasured acids are present
Expected PaCO2 rises 0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3; deviation means an added metabolic problem
Expected HCO3 falls 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg drop in PaCO2; deviation means a mixed disorder
Delta anion gap divided by delta HCO3; a ratio near 1-2 means a mixed disorder
questions.exp: Winter’s formula gives the expected PaCO2 as 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 plus or minus 2; a measured PaCO2 outside that predicted range signals a coexisting respiratory disorder.
why: That expression is the anion gap, which classifies the acidosis rather than predicting compensation.
That rule describes compensation for metabolic alkalosis, where the bicarbonate is elevated.
That is the acute respiratory alkalosis compensation rule, not Winter’s formula.
The delta-delta unmasks a second metabolic process, and a ratio of about 1-2 actually indicates a pure gap acidosis.

questions.q: A patient has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and the urine anion gap (Na + K - Cl) is negative. What does that point to?
ch: A renal cause such as renal tubular acidosis
A high anion gap acidosis from unmeasured acids
A concurrent metabolic alkalosis hidden inside the acidosis
Toxic alcohol ingestion requiring fomepizole
Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss, such as diarrhea
questions.exp: In a non-gap acidosis the urine anion gap separates the causes: a negative value points to gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss such as diarrhea, while a positive value points to a renal cause such as RTA.
why: A positive urine anion gap points to a renal cause like RTA; a negative value points away from it.
The serum gap has already been measured as normal, so unmeasured acids are not the issue.
A concurrent alkalosis is unmasked by the delta-delta ratio, not by the urine anion gap.
Toxic alcohols produce a high anion gap with a high osmolar gap, not a normal-gap acidosis.

questions.q: Why must potassium be monitored especially closely as a metabolic acidosis is corrected?
ch: Bicarbonate raises the serum potassium, so hyperkalemia worsens as the pH normalizes
Potassium binds the unmeasured acids and falsely widens the anion gap
Only patients already on dialysis have clinically important potassium shifts
Correction of the acidosis has no effect on potassium, but the fluids given dilute it
Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells, and insulin or bicarbonate can flip the patient into dangerous hypokalemia
questions.exp: Acidosis shifts K+ out of cells and can present as hyperkalemia; once insulin or bicarbonate is given the potassium moves back into cells, and the module tells you to anticipate that swing — insulin is withheld in DKA if the K is below 3.3.
why: Bicarbonate drives potassium intracellularly and risks hypokalemia rather than worsening hyperkalemia.
Potassium is not part of the module’s anion gap and does not bind the unmeasured acids.
The swing is expected whenever an acidosis is corrected, which is why the module pre-empts it in the DKA plan.
Correction drives potassium back into cells; the module emphasizes that transcellular shift, not dilution.

questions.q: When does the module support giving intravenous sodium bicarbonate in metabolic acidosis?
ch: Routinely in lactic acidosis in order to restore tissue perfusion
In any acidosis with a pH below 7.35 to normalize the bicarbonate
For severe acidemia generally below a pH of 7.1, severe non-gap acidosis or RTA, and specific toxins such as salicylate or TCA
Whenever the calculated anion gap exceeds 12 mEq/L, regardless of the pH
Routinely in every case of DKA in order to close the anion gap faster
questions.exp: Sodium bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidemia (generally a pH below 7.1), severe non-gap acidosis or RTA, and specific toxins such as salicylate or TCA; it is not routine in DKA or lactic acidosis and risks hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, volume overload, and paradoxical CNS acidosis.
why: Bicarbonate is not routine in lactic acidosis either — fluids and source control restore perfusion.
A pH below 7.35 merely defines the disorder; alkali is reserved for far more severe acidemia.
A gap above 12 simply classifies the acidosis and is not by itself an indication for alkali.
Bicarbonate is explicitly not routine in DKA; insulin with dextrose and potassium is the definitive therapy that halts ketogenesis.

questions.q: A patient has a high anion gap acidosis with no lactate or ketone source, and the osmolar gap is markedly elevated. What is the next step?
ch: Recalculate the anion gap corrected for albumin and observe
Start intravenous insulin with dextrose and potassium to halt ketogenesis
Give large-volume 0.9% saline and recheck the anion gap in the morning
Give fomepizole early for suspected methanol or ethylene glycol, with hemodialysis in severe cases
Start oral sodium citrate to keep the serum bicarbonate near normal
questions.exp: A high anion gap plus a high osmolar gap screams methanol or ethylene glycol: give fomepizole early to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase, with hemodialysis to clear the toxin and correct the acidosis in severe cases.
why: Albumin correction can uncover a hidden acidosis but does nothing about a toxic alcohol already flagged by the osmolar gap.
Ketogenesis is not the problem here, because ketones were already absent.
Delay is unsafe with a toxic alcohol, and large-volume normal saline can itself add a hyperchloremic non-gap acidosis.
Oral alkali is for chronic non-gap acidosis from RTA or CKD, not for an acute toxic ingestion.

questions.q: A patient in DKA with deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations becomes quieter, breathing more slowly and shallowly. How should this be interpreted?
ch: As the expected effect of sodium bicarbonate on the respiratory drive
As a superimposed respiratory alkalosis from anxiety
As evidence that the acidosis was a non-gap hyperchloremic process all along
As failing compensation and impending respiratory failure rather than improvement
As successful correction of the acidosis now that the anion gap is closing
questions.exp: Kussmaul respirations are the bedside signature of severe metabolic acidosis; a tiring patient whose Kussmaul breathing slows or stops is a red flag for failing compensation and impending respiratory failure, not recovery.
why: Bicarbonate is not routine in DKA, and a slowing respiratory pattern here reflects fatigue rather than a drug effect.
Anxious hyperventilation would increase, not decrease, the rate and depth of breathing.
The breathing pattern reflects compensation and fatigue, not whether the anion gap is wide or normal.
The module warns explicitly that a patient who stops Kussmaul breathing may be tiring toward respiratory failure, not improving.

questions.q: In a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, a delta-delta ratio (delta AG / delta HCO3) greater than 2 suggests what?
ch: A concurrent metabolic alkalosis hidden inside the gap acidosis
A concurrent non-gap hyperchloremic acidosis
An inappropriate degree of respiratory compensation
Hypoalbuminemia that is falsely lowering the anion gap
A pure high anion gap acidosis with no second process present
questions.exp: The delta-delta ratio in a gap acidosis: about 1-2 is a pure gap acidosis, below 1 suggests a concurrent non-gap acidosis, and above 2 suggests a concurrent metabolic alkalosis.
why: A ratio below 1 is what suggests a concurrent non-gap acidosis.
Respiratory compensation is judged against Winter’s formula, not the delta-delta ratio.
Low albumin is handled separately by adding about 2.5 to the gap per 1 g/dL fall below 4.
A ratio of roughly 1-2 is what indicates a pure gap acidosis.

questions.q: Which arterial blood gas pattern defines metabolic alkalosis?
ch: A pH above 7.45 with a PaCO2 below 35 mmHg and a low HCO3-
A pH below 7.35 with HCO3- below 22 mEq/L and a low PaCO2
A pH below 7.35 with a PaCO2 above 45 mmHg and a raised HCO3-
A normal pH with a high HCO3- and an unchanged PaCO2
A pH above 7.45 with HCO3- above 26 mEq/L and a compensatory rise in PaCO2
questions.exp: Metabolic alkalosis is a primary elevation in HCO3-: a pH above 7.45 with HCO3- above 26 mEq/L and compensatory hypoventilation raising the PaCO2 about 0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate.
why: That is respiratory alkalosis, in which hyperventilation lowers the PaCO2 and the bicarbonate falls.
A low bicarbonate with acidemia and compensatory hypocapnia is metabolic acidosis.
A primary rise in PaCO2 with acidemia is respiratory acidosis, where the kidney retains bicarbonate.
Metabolic alkalosis raises the pH, and compensation raises the PaCO2 rather than leaving it unchanged.

questions.q: Which single test is the most useful in classifying metabolic alkalosis?
ch: The urine anion gap (Na + K - Cl)
The urine sodium concentration
The serum anion gap
The urine chloride concentration
The serum osmolar gap
questions.exp: The single most useful test is the urine chloride: below 20 mEq/L means saline-responsive disease (chloride and volume depleted), and above 20 mEq/L means saline-resistant disease.
why: The urine anion gap separates GI from renal causes of a non-gap metabolic acidosis.
Diuretics and vomiting can spuriously raise the urine sodium, so chloride better reflects effective volume.
The anion gap classifies metabolic acidosis; it plays no part in this split.
The osmolar gap is used when toxic alcohols are suspected in a gap acidosis.

questions.q: Which cause of metabolic alkalosis is both the most common and saline-responsive?
ch: Vomiting or nasogastric suction
Bartter or Gitelman syndrome
Licorice ingestion causing mineralocorticoid excess
Cushing syndrome with cortisol excess
Primary hyperaldosteronism with hypertension
questions.exp: Vomiting and NG suction are the most common cause and are saline-responsive: loss of HCl generates the alkalosis, and volume, chloride, and potassium depletion maintain it.
why: These tubulopathies are saline-resistant and normotensive, with a high urine chloride.
Licorice acts like a mineralocorticoid and produces saline-resistant alkalosis.
Cushing syndrome is listed among the saline-resistant, mineralocorticoid-excess causes.
Hyperaldosteronism is the classic saline-resistant cause, with a urine chloride above 20 mEq/L.

questions.q: A vomiting patient has an alkalemic blood pH but an acidic urine. What explains this paradoxical aciduria?
ch: The kidney is excreting the excess bicarbonate as fast as it is being generated
An unrecognized concurrent high anion gap metabolic acidosis is present
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition from an antacid the patient is taking
Hyperkalemia is driving hydrogen ions into the renal tubular cells
Volume and potassium depletion with secondary hyperaldosteronism force H+ excretion to reclaim Na+
questions.exp: In the vomiting patient, loss of HCl generates the alkalosis and then volume, chloride, and potassium depletion with secondary hyperaldosteronism maintain it — forcing H+ excretion to reclaim Na+ and producing an acidic urine despite alkalemia.
why: If the kidney could dump the bicarbonate the alkalosis would not be maintained at all, and the urine would be alkaline.
The acidic urine here is explained by the maintenance mechanism rather than by a second acid load.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition produces a bicarbonate diuresis and an alkaline urine.
The vomiting patient is hypokalemic, and it is that potassium depletion which sustains H+ secretion.

questions.q: A patient with heart failure and volume overload develops a diuretic-induced metabolic alkalosis, and saline cannot safely be given. What is the appropriate treatment?
ch: Ammonium chloride, which is safe in essentially all patients
Acetazolamide, which promotes a bicarbonate diuresis
0.9% sodium chloride at a high infusion rate
Spironolactone for mineralocorticoid excess
Intravenous hydrochloric acid through a peripheral line
questions.exp: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that promotes a bicarbonate diuresis, and it is the module’s answer when saline cannot be given — as in CHF with diuretic-induced alkalosis. Monitor potassium, because it can worsen hypokalemia.
why: Ammonium chloride is a specialist last resort and is contraindicated in hepatic failure.
Saline is first-line only when the volume load can be tolerated; here it risks worsening the overload.
Aldosterone antagonists target saline-resistant mineralocorticoid-excess states, not diuretic-induced contraction alkalosis.
HCl is reserved for severe refractory alkalosis with a pH above 7.55 and requires a central line and ICU monitoring.

questions.q: Metabolic alkalosis requires both a generation phase and a maintenance phase. What does the maintenance phase imply?
ch: Something is blocking renal bicarbonate excretion: volume depletion, chloride depletion, hypokalemia, or mineralocorticoid excess
Total body potassium is elevated, driving hydrogen ions into the cells
The lungs have stopped compensating for the elevated serum bicarbonate
An acid load is being added to the blood continuously from the tissues
The kidney is excreting bicarbonate faster than it can possibly be produced
questions.exp: The kidney normally dumps excess bicarbonate rapidly, so persistence implies that something is blocking renal bicarbonate excretion — volume depletion, chloride depletion, hypokalemia, or mineralocorticoid excess.
why: Hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, is the near-universal finding, and it sustains the alkalosis.
Compensatory hypoventilation is part of the disorder itself, not the reason the alkalosis persists.
A continuous acid load causes acidosis; alkalosis is generated by acid loss or bicarbonate gain.
Rapid renal bicarbonate excretion is exactly what normally terminates a metabolic alkalosis.

questions.q: A hypertensive patient has hypokalemia, a metabolic alkalosis, and a urine chloride of 45 mEq/L. What is the best next step?
ch: Give a large bolus of isotonic saline and recheck the bicarbonate
Start acetazolamide to induce a bicarbonate diuresis
Check an aldosterone-to-renin ratio for mineralocorticoid excess
Start a proton pump inhibitor to reduce gastric acid loss
Order genetic testing for Bartter or Gitelman syndrome first
questions.exp: Hypertension plus hypokalemia plus metabolic alkalosis with a urine chloride above 20 mEq/L is saline-resistant mineralocorticoid excess; the module’s move is an aldosterone:renin ratio rather than reflexively giving saline.
why: A urine chloride above 20 mEq/L marks saline-resistant disease, in which saline is ineffective.
Acetazolamide is the workaround when saline cannot be given, not the diagnostic step in a hypertensive, resistant patient.
A PPI limits ongoing generation in vomiting or NG suction, which is not the picture described here.
Those tubulopathies also raise the urine chloride but characteristically present with normotension, not hypertension.

questions.q: Why will the pH often not normalize until the potassium is repleted, and why is potassium chloride the preferred salt?
ch: Potassium is required for carbonic anhydrase activity, which the chloride blocks
Hyperkalemia perpetuates the alkalosis, so potassium must be driven into cells
The potassium raises the urine chloride and converts resistant to responsive disease
Hypokalemia both causes and sustains the alkalosis, and the chloride salt also repairs the chloride depletion
Potassium buffers hydrogen ions directly in the plasma, and the chloride is inert
questions.exp: Chloride depletion and hypokalemia are the unifying drivers, both stimulating distal H+ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption, so the chloride salt is preferred because it repairs the potassium and the chloride deficit at once.
why: Carbonic anhydrase is the target of acetazolamide; that is not why KCl is the chosen salt.
Hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, is the near-universal finding in metabolic alkalosis.
Urine chloride is a diagnostic marker of the underlying mechanism, not a treatment target to be manipulated.
The module’s mechanism is stimulation of distal H+ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption, and the chloride is itself therapeutic.

questions.q: Which finding in metabolic alkalosis represents a medical emergency?
ch: Gynecomastia developing in a patient taking spironolactone
A urine chloride below 20 mEq/L in a patient who has been vomiting
Severe alkalemia with a pH above 7.55 accompanied by arrhythmias, seizures, or tetany
A PaCO2 that has risen 0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate
A serum chloride at the low end of normal with a normal potassium
questions.exp: Severe alkalemia with a pH above 7.55 accompanied by arrhythmias, seizures, tetany, or altered mental status is a medical emergency, and it is the setting in which HCl or ammonium chloride is considered.
why: Gynecomastia is a recognized spironolactone side effect, not an acid-base emergency.
That simply classifies the alkalosis as saline-responsive, the most common and most readily treated form.
That is precisely the expected, appropriate compensation for the disorder.
A low chloride is characteristic of the disorder and is not by itself an emergency.

questions.q: A patient with metabolic alkalosis and limited respiratory reserve is prescribed a sedative. Why should the nurse question the order?
ch: Sedatives interfere with the accuracy of the urine chloride measurement
Compensatory hypoventilation is already depressing breathing, and a sedative can blunt it further and produce hypoxemia
Sedatives increase the risk of gynecomastia when combined with spironolactone
Sedatives raise the serum bicarbonate and deepen the alkalosis directly
Sedatives cause a bicarbonate diuresis with unpredictable potassium loss
questions.exp: Metabolic alkalosis is compensated by hypoventilation, and marked compensatory hypoventilation can itself produce hypoxemia in a patient with limited respiratory reserve — so the module says to hold or question sedatives that could blunt an already-depressed respiratory drive.
why: Nothing in the module ties sedatives to the interpretation of a urine chloride.
Gynecomastia is a spironolactone effect and is unrelated to sedation or to acid-base status.
The concern is respiratory depression added on top of compensatory hypoventilation, not a direct effect on bicarbonate.
A bicarbonate diuresis with potassium loss describes acetazolamide, not a sedative.

questions.q: Which arterial blood gas values define respiratory acidosis?
ch: A PaCO2 above 45 mmHg with a pH above 7.45
A PaCO2 above 45 mmHg with a pH below 7.35
A PaCO2 below 35 mmHg with a pH above 7.45
An HCO3- below 22 mEq/L with a pH below 7.35
An HCO3- above 26 mEq/L with a pH above 7.45
questions.exp: Respiratory acidosis is defined by a PaCO2 above 45 mmHg with a pH below 7.35, caused by inadequate alveolar ventilation that lets carbonic acid accumulate.
why: In a respiratory disorder pH and PaCO2 move in opposite directions — ROME: Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal.
A low PaCO2 with alkalemia is respiratory alkalosis from alveolar hyperventilation.
A primary fall in bicarbonate defines metabolic acidosis.
A primary rise in bicarbonate defines metabolic alkalosis.

questions.q: The module groups the causes of respiratory acidosis into which three categories?
ch: Transcellular shift, decreased gut absorption, and renal wasting
A generation phase, a maintenance phase, and a correction phase
Saline-responsive, saline-resistant, and mixed disease
Won’t breathe, can’t breathe, and pump failure
Acid gain, bicarbonate loss, and impaired renal acid excretion
questions.exp: Causes are framed by the defect: won’t breathe (CNS or opioid-benzodiazepine depression, brainstem lesion), can’t breathe (COPD, severe asthma, pneumothorax, obesity hypoventilation), or pump failure (Guillain-Barre, myasthenia gravis, kyphoscoliosis).
why: That framework belongs to phosphate disorders, not to a ventilation problem.
Generation and maintenance phases are the framework for metabolic alkalosis.
The saline-responsive split classifies metabolic alkalosis by urine chloride.
Those are the three mechanisms of metabolic acidosis.

questions.q: Which cluster of findings is the classic bedside sign of dangerous hypercapnia?
ch: Muscle weakness, hemolysis, and rhabdomyolysis
Tetany, carpopedal spasm, and perioral tingling
Kussmaul respirations with a widened anion gap
Chvostek and Trousseau signs with pruritus
Somnolence, headache, and asterixis
questions.exp: CO2 narcosis — somnolence, headache, and asterixis — is the classic sign of dangerous hypercapnia; flushed warm skin and accessory muscle use are also described on exam.
why: That cluster is the presentation of severe hypophosphatemia.
Those are the neuromuscular signs of alkalosis with a reduced ionized calcium.
Deep Kussmaul breathing is the bedside signature of severe metabolic acidosis, not of CO2 retention.
Those reflect hypocalcemia, classically from hyperphosphatemia.

questions.q: An arterial blood gas shows a PaCO2 of 80 mmHg with an HCO3- of 34 mEq/L and only a mildly reduced pH. How is this best classified?
ch: Acute respiratory acidosis, since HCO3- rises about 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg of PaCO2
Chronic respiratory acidosis, since HCO3- rises about 3-4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg of PaCO2
A primary metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation
A pure respiratory alkalosis with renal bicarbonate wasting
A normal gas that requires no further interpretation
questions.exp: A markedly elevated HCO3- with only a mildly low pH indicates chronic respiratory acidosis: the kidneys retain bicarbonate over 3-5 days, raising it about 3-4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg of PaCO2 versus only about 1 mEq/L acutely.
why: An acute 40 mmHg rise would lift the bicarbonate only about 4 mEq/L and would drop the pH sharply.
Compensatory hypoventilation for an alkalosis would come with an elevated pH, not a reduced one.
Respiratory alkalosis features a low PaCO2 with a raised pH and a falling bicarbonate.
A PaCO2 of 80 mmHg with a low pH is markedly abnormal by the module’s own definition.

questions.q: What SpO2 target does the module set for a COPD patient with chronic hypercapnia, and why?
ch: 92-96%, because that range protects tissue oxygen delivery in every patient
Above 98%, because a fully normal saturation is always the safest goal
88-92%, because excessive oxygen worsens CO2 retention and blunts respiratory drive
80-85%, because permissive hypoxemia stimulates the respiratory centre
Any value at all, provided the patient is receiving BiPAP at the time
questions.exp: In chronic COPD hypercapnia the target SpO2 is 88-92%: excessive oxygen worsens CO2 retention through V/Q mismatch, the Haldane effect, and reduced respiratory drive, and chasing a normal saturation can tip a retainer into hypercapnic coma.
why: 92-96% is the target used for hypoxemia-driven hyperventilation, not for a known CO2 retainer.
Chasing a normal saturation is exactly what can tip a retainer into hypercapnic coma.
The module never endorses a saturation that low; the stated target is 88-92%.
Oxygen is titrated to the prescribed target whether or not noninvasive ventilation is running.

questions.q: A COPD patient in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure is alert and protecting the airway. What is the evidence-based first move?
ch: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH
Flumazenil to reverse any sedative contribution
Noninvasive ventilation with BiPAP
Immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation
High-flow oxygen titrated to an SpO2 above 98%
questions.exp: Noninvasive ventilation with BiPAP is the evidence-based first move in COPD-related acute hypercapnic failure and often prevents intubation; it is avoided if the patient cannot protect the airway or is obtunded.
why: Nothing in this module supports alkali for hypercapnia — the fix is restoring alveolar ventilation.
Flumazenil reverses isolated benzodiazepine hypoventilation and can precipitate seizures in chronic users or mixed overdose.
Intubation is the definitive support reserved for failure of noninvasive ventilation or an unprotected airway.
Over-oxygenating a retainer worsens CO2 retention; the target in chronic hypercapnia is 88-92%.

questions.q: An opioid overdose patient has a PaCO2 of 70 mmHg and a respiratory rate of 6. How should naloxone be used?
ch: Give a single large dose to achieve full arousal and then simply observe
Withhold it and proceed directly to intubation in every such case
Substitute flumazenil, which reverses both opioids and benzodiazepines
Give it only once the arterial pH has fallen below 7.20
Titrate it to restore respirations rather than full arousal, expecting to redose because its half-life is short
questions.exp: Naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression — the "won’t breathe" category — and is titrated to restore respirations rather than full arousal; its short half-life means re-narcotization and repeat dosing or an infusion may be needed.
why: Naloxone is titrated to respirations, and its short half-life means re-narcotization can follow one large dose.
This is a "won’t breathe" problem with a specific reversal agent; intubation is for failure or an unprotected airway.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines only, and it carries a seizure risk in chronic users or mixed overdose.
A pH below 7.20 is already a decompensation red flag; a reversal agent is not held back waiting for it.

questions.q: Why must a chronically elevated PaCO2 not be lowered too quickly on mechanical ventilation?
ch: Rapid correction causes post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis and seizures
Rapid correction triggers rebound cerebral vasodilation and raised ICP
Rapid correction causes a hyperchloremic non-gap metabolic acidosis
Rapid correction drives potassium out of cells and causes hyperkalemia
Rapid correction abolishes the compensatory rise in the PaO2
questions.exp: The kidneys have retained bicarbonate to buffer the chronic hypercapnia, so dropping the PaCO2 quickly leaves that bicarbonate unopposed and causes post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis and seizures.
why: That caution applies to correcting chronic hypocapnia in respiratory alkalosis, not chronic hypercapnia.
Hyperchloremic non-gap acidosis comes from bicarbonate loss or large-volume saline, not from correcting hypercapnia.
The hazard the module names for fast correction is post-hypercapnic alkalosis with seizures, not a potassium shift.
Oxygenation is managed with titrated oxygen; the hazard here is the retained bicarbonate left behind.

questions.q: A patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome is being watched for hypercapnic respiratory failure. Which bedside measurements best track the ventilatory pump?
ch: Chvostek and Trousseau signs at the bedside
Glasgow Coma Scale score and pupillary response
Urine chloride and serum potassium trends
Negative inspiratory force and vital capacity
Serum anion gap and osmolar gap calculations
questions.exp: For neuromuscular pump failure such as Guillain-Barre or myasthenia gravis the module’s bedside tools are negative inspiratory force and vital capacity, while the Glasgow Coma Scale is used for a depressed respiratory drive.
why: Those test for neuromuscular irritability from a low ionized calcium, not for pump strength.
The Glasgow Coma Scale is the module’s tool for a depressed respiratory drive, not for ventilatory muscle strength.
Those are metabolic alkalosis measures and say nothing about respiratory muscle strength.
Those calculations belong to the metabolic acidosis workup.

questions.q: A fatiguing asthmatic on BiPAP develops a silent chest, paradoxical abdominal breathing, and a falling respiratory rate. What does this indicate?
ch: Imminent pump failure requiring escalation to intubation
Development of a superimposed respiratory alkalosis
An expected effect of controlled oxygen at an SpO2 of 88-92%
Post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis from too-rapid correction
Successful noninvasive ventilation with resolving bronchospasm
questions.exp: A silent chest, paradoxical (abdominal) breathing, or a falling respiratory rate in a fatiguing patient are red flags for imminent pump failure — the module’s explicit trigger to escalate to intubation when noninvasive ventilation is failing.
why: An alkalosis would require increased alveolar ventilation, the opposite of what is happening here.
Titrated oxygen at the target saturation does not produce a silent chest or paradoxical breathing.
That complication follows rapid lowering of a chronically high PaCO2, not clinical fatigue.
A silent chest with a falling rate in a fatiguing patient is a sign of failure, not of resolution.

questions.q: Which arterial blood gas pattern defines respiratory alkalosis?
ch: A PaCO2 above 45 mmHg with a pH below 7.35
An HCO3 above 26 mEq/L with a pH above 7.45
A PaCO2 below 35 mmHg with a pH above 7.45
An HCO3 below 22 mEq/L with a pH below 7.35
A PaCO2 below 35 mmHg with a pH below 7.35
questions.exp: Respiratory alkalosis is defined by a PaCO2 less than 35 mmHg with a resulting pH greater than 7.45, produced when alveolar ventilation exceeds metabolic CO2 production.
why: That is respiratory acidosis from alveolar hypoventilation.
A primary rise in bicarbonate is metabolic alkalosis.
A primary fall in bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis.
A low PaCO2 with acidemia is respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, which the ABG is used to distinguish from a primary alkalosis.

questions.q: The mnemonic CHAMPS covers the causes of respiratory alkalosis. What does it stand for?
ch: CNS disease, Hypoxia, Anxiety, Mechanical ventilation, Progesterone/Pregnancy, Salicylates/Sepsis
Chloride depletion, Hypokalemia, Aldosterone excess, Milk-alkali, Pyloric stenosis, Suction
Cushing, Hyperaldosteronism, Antacids, Milk-alkali, Post-hypercapnia, Saline resistance
Cannot breathe, Hypoventilation, Airway obstruction, Myasthenia, Pump failure, Sedatives
Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates
questions.exp: CHAMPS: CNS disease, Hypoxia, Anxiety, Mechanical ventilation, Progesterone/Pregnancy, Salicylates/Sepsis.
why: Those are drivers of metabolic alkalosis, not of hyperventilation.
That list is assembled from metabolic alkalosis causes rather than causes of hypocapnia.
Those describe the hypoventilation categories of respiratory acidosis.
That expansion is MUDPILES, the high anion gap metabolic acidosis differential.

questions.q: A young anxious patient is hyperventilating with tingling fingers. Which intervention does the module explicitly forbid?
ch: Screening for hypoxemia with pulse oximetry
A short-term benzodiazepine once organic causes are excluded
Staying at the bedside throughout the episode
Paper-bag rebreathing to raise the PaCO2
Reassurance with coached, paced breathing
questions.exp: Paper-bag rebreathing is explicitly forbidden — it risks fatal hypoxia and can mask a serious cause such as PE or DKA; instead coach slow, controlled breathing and stay with the patient.
why: Assessing oxygenation first is exactly what the module prioritizes, because the patient may be hypoxic from PE.
A benzodiazepine is an accepted cautious adjunct for severe panic-driven hyperventilation refractory to coaching.
Staying with the patient is part of the recommended nursing response.
Coached, paced breathing with reassurance is the first-line treatment for acute anxiety-driven hyperventilation.

questions.q: A hyperventilating patient has perioral and digital paresthesias with carpopedal spasm, yet the total serum calcium is normal. What explains the symptoms?
ch: Cerebral vasoconstriction from hypocapnia is producing the tingling
Alkalemia increases albumin’s affinity for calcium, lowering the ionized fraction
Hyperkalemia is increasing neuromuscular excitability
The total calcium result is spurious and should be corrected for albumin
Hypophosphatemia from a transcellular shift is causing the spasm
questions.exp: Alkalemia increases albumin’s affinity for calcium, so the ionized calcium falls while the total calcium stays normal — producing neuromuscular irritability with perioral and fingertip tingling and carpopedal spasm.
why: Cerebral vasoconstriction explains the lightheadedness and syncope, not the perioral and digital paresthesias and spasm.
Respiratory alkalosis trends toward mild hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.
The total calcium genuinely stays normal; it is the ionized fraction that falls.
Mild hypophosphatemia can accompany respiratory alkalosis, but the module attributes the paresthesias to a reduced ionized calcium.

questions.q: How does the expected bicarbonate response differ between acute and chronic respiratory alkalosis?
ch: HCO3 rises about 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg acutely and about 3-4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg when chronic
HCO3 falls about 4-5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg acutely and about 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg when chronic
The PaCO2 is expected to rise 0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3 in both
The expected PaCO2 is 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 plus or minus 2 in both acute and chronic disease
HCO3 falls about 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg drop in PaCO2 acutely and about 4-5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg when chronic
questions.exp: Acute respiratory alkalosis has minimal renal compensation, with HCO3 falling about 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg drop in PaCO2; chronic disease involves renal HCO3 wasting, with HCO3 falling about 4-5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg drop.
why: Those are the compensation rules for respiratory acidosis, where a rising PaCO2 raises the bicarbonate.
The values are reversed: renal bicarbonate wasting takes days, so the larger fall is the chronic one.
That rule describes the expected compensation for a metabolic alkalosis.
Winter’s formula predicts compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not for hypocapnia.

questions.q: A patient with tinnitus is tachypneic, the ABG shows a low PaCO2, and there is a high anion gap. What is the classic explanation?
ch: High-altitude hypocapnia being treated with acetazolamide
Pure anxiety-driven hyperventilation with an otherwise normal chemistry panel
Salicylate toxicity, which stimulates the medulla and simultaneously causes an anion-gap acidosis
Pregnancy-related chronic respiratory alkalosis from progesterone
Iatrogenic over-ventilation from the mechanical ventilator settings
questions.exp: Salicylate toxicity independently stimulates the medulla to produce a respiratory alkalosis AND causes an anion-gap metabolic acidosis — a mixed picture with tinnitus that the module names as the board favorite and a red flag needing urgent management.
why: Altitude hypocapnia is hypoxia-driven, acetazolamide is given to aid acclimatization, and tinnitus is not part of the picture.
Anxiety does not widen the anion gap, and the module treats it as a diagnosis of exclusion.
Progesterone-driven hyperventilation is a normal chronic hypocapnia without a wide anion gap or tinnitus.
Over-ventilation lowers the PaCO2 but adds no unmeasured acids and causes no tinnitus.

questions.q: A patient with pneumonia is hyperventilating because of hypoxemia. How should oxygen be used?
ch: Titrate oxygen to an SpO2 of 88-92 percent as in chronic hypercapnia
Give a benzodiazepine first and add oxygen only if it fails
Apply paper-bag rebreathing to bring the PaCO2 back toward normal
Give supplemental oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 92-96 percent to relieve the hypoxic drive
Withhold oxygen so that the hypoxic respiratory drive is preserved
questions.exp: Supplemental oxygen corrects hypoxemia-driven hyperventilation from PE, pneumonia, or altitude by relieving the hypoxic respiratory drive; titrate to an SpO2 of 92-96 percent and reassess.
why: 88-92 percent is the COPD retainer target in respiratory acidosis, not the target this module gives.
A benzodiazepine is reserved for severe panic-driven hyperventilation once organic causes have been excluded.
Paper-bag rebreathing risks fatal hypoxia and is never used, least of all in a hypoxemic patient.
Relieving the hypoxic drive is the therapeutic goal here, and oxygen is the specific treatment for hypoxemia-driven hyperventilation.

questions.q: A tachypneic patient with pleuritic chest pain and hypoxemia is labelled "anxiety" by the team. What is the correct stance?
ch: Attribute the paresthesias to hyperkalemia and recheck the potassium
Reduce the ventilator rate in order to raise the PaCO2
Accept the label and begin coached breathing with reassurance
Give lorazepam immediately to break the hyperventilation cycle
Exclude PE, sepsis, DKA, and a CNS event first, because anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion
questions.exp: Hyperventilation with hypoxemia or pleuritic chest pain should prompt suspicion of pulmonary embolism or pneumonia rather than anxiety — the module insists anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion once PE, sepsis, DKA, CNS events, and hypoxemia are ruled out.
why: The paresthesias come from a reduced ionized calcium, and respiratory alkalosis trends toward hypokalemia.
Adjusting settings applies to iatrogenic over-ventilation on mechanical support, which is not the situation here.
Coaching is right for true psychogenic hyperventilation, but hypoxemia with pleuritic pain points to an organic cause.
A benzodiazepine is used only after organic causes are excluded and can itself depress respiration.

questions.q: A ventilated patient with chronic hypocapnia is being weaned toward a normal PaCO2. What caution applies?
ch: Add acetazolamide to accelerate the rise in the PaCO2
Raise the PaCO2 gradually to avoid rebound cerebral vasodilation and increased ICP
Increase the set respiratory rate to shorten the weaning period
Raise the PaCO2 quickly, since hypocapnia has no cerebral vascular effects
Correct it slowly to avoid post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis and seizures
questions.exp: For iatrogenic over-ventilation, lower the respiratory rate or tidal volume to raise the PaCO2 — but correct the PaCO2 gradually in chronic hypocapnia to avoid rebound cerebral vasodilation and increased ICP.
why: Acetazolamide is used for high-altitude illness and causes a mild metabolic acidosis; it is not a tool for raising PaCO2.
Raising the rate lowers the PaCO2 further and worsens the iatrogenic hypocapnia.
Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction, and correcting it abruptly is what risks rebound vasodilation.
That hazard belongs to lowering a chronically high PaCO2 in respiratory acidosis, not to raising a chronically low one.

questions.q: Beyond the change in pH, what effect does alkalemia have on oxygen delivery in respiratory alkalosis?
ch: It shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly and tissue offloading falls
It shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve right, improving tissue oxygen offloading
It has no effect on the oxyhemoglobin curve, only on the ionized calcium
It raises 2,3-DPG production and so increases oxygen release to tissues
It dilates cerebral vessels, raising cerebral blood flow and oxygen supply
questions.exp: Alkalosis shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly and tissue offloading is reduced; cerebral vasoconstriction additionally lowers cerebral blood flow, explaining lightheadedness and syncope.
why: Alkalosis shifts the curve left, which reduces rather than improves tissue oxygen delivery.
The module describes both a left-shifted curve and a fall in the ionized calcium.
2,3-DPG is discussed under phosphate depletion, and the effect described here is a left shift that holds oxygen more tightly.
Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and lowers cerebral blood flow, which is why patients feel lightheaded.
